w: Parthasarathy means 'charioteer of Arjuna' -- Krishna's Mahabharata role -- and this 6th-century temple built by Pallava king Narasimhavarman I stacks five forms of Vishnu under one roof, from Rama to Yoga Narasimha. One of 108 Divya Desams sung by the Alvar poet-saints, and one of Chennai's oldest structures.
s: Krishna the charioteer, five ways, since the 6th century.
_facts: 6th-century Hindu Vaishnavite temple built by Pallava king Narasimhavarman I
houses five forms of Vishnu including Yoga Narasimha, Rama, Krishna as Parthasarathy
one of 108 Divya Desams named in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham
name means charioteer of Arjuna, referencing Krishna's role in the Mahabharata

w: A patch of scrub and lake wedged inside a metropolis of millions -- Guindy is one of India's smallest national parks, yet somehow still runs free-ranging herds of 400 blackbuck and 2,000 spotted deer alongside jackals and 130-odd bird species. It grew out of the grounds around Raj Bhavan and never really left.
s: 400 blackbuck roaming wild inside the city limits.
_facts: 2.70 sq km, one of India's smallest national parks, inside a metro area
extension of the grounds around Raj Bhavan, official residence of the Governor of Tamil Nadu
home to 400 blackbucks, 2,000 spotted deer, 24 jackals, over 130 bird species

w: One of the largest mosques in India, standing right on Anna Salai, this Shi'ite mosque is a major centre of azadari -- the ritual mourning observances of Shia Islam -- drawing Chennai's Shia community for its most solemn gatherings of the year.
s: Chennai's grand stage for Shia mourning rites.
_facts: Shi'ite mosque on Anna Salai, Chennai
one of the largest mosques in India
revered place of worship and azadari for Shia Muslims

w: William Petrie set up a private observatory here in 1786; the East India Company took it over six years later and ran it for the better part of 140 years, timing ships and mapping stars for the Company's trade network. It produced a comprehensive star catalogue -- then in 1931, it simply closed.
s: The East India Company's star-mapping outpost, 1792-1931.
_facts: Private observatory set up by William Petrie in 1786
managed by the British East India Company from 1792
purpose was navigation, latitude, and time standards, later stars and geomagnetism
ran from around 1792 to 1931, produced a comprehensive star catalogue

w: The first English fortress ever built in India, raised in 1639 on what was then empty coast -- the city we now call Chennai grew up entirely around it afterward. Once called White Town, the fort still does government work today: it houses the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly behind its original walls.
s: The fort Chennai grew up around, doing government work.
_facts: Founded 1639, first English (later British) fortress in India
historically known as White Town
the city of Madras/Chennai evolved around the fortress
currently houses the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly

w: The story goes that Parvati once worshipped Shiva here as a peahen -- mayil in Tamil -- supposedly how Mylapore got its name. The temple dates to around the 7th century and gets a namecheck in the Tevaram, the canonical hymnbook of Tamil Shaiva saint-poets. Six rituals a day, still, more than a millennium on.
s: The peahen legend that gave Mylapore its name.
_facts: 7th-century Hindu temple to Shiva in Mylapore
legend that Parvati worshipped Shiva as a peahen (mayil), giving the area its name
mentioned in the Tevaram, the Tamil Shaiva canon of the Nayanar saint-poets
six daily rituals, four yearly festivals

w: Opened in 1851, second-oldest museum in the country -- and it holds one of the largest collections of Roman coins found outside Europe, alongside 500 bronze idols dating back three thousand years. The Indo-Saracenic building also folds in the National Art Gallery, hung with Raja Ravi Varma canvases.
_facts: Started 1851, second-oldest museum in India after Kolkata's Indian Museum
among the largest collections of Roman currency outside Europe
500 bronze idols dating to 1000 BCE
Indo-Saracenic building housing the National Art Gallery with Raja Ravi Varma paintings

w: For almost a century this was where the Nawab of Arcot actually lived and ruled from, 1768 to 1855 -- one of the earliest big Indo-Saracenic statements in the city, blending British and Deccan architectural instincts before the style became a Chennai signature.
s: Where the Nawab of Arcot ruled for nearly a century.
_facts: Official residence of the Nawab of Arcot from 1768 to 1855
constructed in Indo-Saracenic architectural style

w: An all-white neoclassical wedding cake of a building, mixing Ionic and Corinthian columns to house the Greater Chennai Corporation, a stone's throw from Chennai Central station. City hall, doing double duty as its own architectural flex.
s: The all-white neoclassical seat of the city's government.
_facts: Seat and headquarters of the Greater Chennai Corporation
neoclassical architecture combining Ionic and Corinthian styles
all-white structure located near Chennai Central railway station

w: Rukmini Devi Arundale and her husband George founded this academy in 1936 to preserve classical Bharatanatyam dance and Gandharvaveda music with rigor and 'perfectionism.' It moved to a 40-hectare campus in Besant Nagar in 1962, and in 1994 an Act of Parliament made it a formal Institute of National Importance.
s: A dance and music academy ranked by Act of Parliament.
_facts: Founded January 1936 by Rukmini Devi Arundale and George Arundale
dedicated to Bharatanatyam dance and Gandharvaveda music
moved to a 40-hectare campus in Besant Nagar in 1962
recognised as an Institute of National Importance by Act of Parliament in 1994

w: Built purely to honour one figure -- the classical Tamil poet-philosopher Valluvar -- this monument doubles as the city's biggest Tamil cultural centre. A whole building raised in tribute to a single writer says something about how seriously Chennai takes its literary history.
s: A monument built for one poet, and only one poet.
_facts: Monument dedicated to the classical Tamil poet-philosopher Valluvar
the city's biggest Tamil cultural centre

w: Built under British rule to link nearly 800km of coastal backwaters to Chennai's port, this canal did brisk trade until railways and roads made it redundant -- long stretches silted up and turned foul over the 20th century. Lately it's being eyed again as a buffer against tsunamis and cyclones, not as a trade route.
s: 800km of British-era canal, now eyed as a flood buffer.
_facts: 796 km freshwater navigation canal built during British rule
connected coastal backwaters to Chennai port
declined with rise of rail and road transport, became polluted in parts
renewed interest for flood, tsunami and cyclone protection; 2021 rehabilitation pledge

w: Opened only in 2012, this Gaudiya Vaishnavism temple -- the Sri Sri Radha Krishna Mandir -- is one of the newest major religious landmarks in the city, dedicated to Krishna and his consort Radha and built to the devotional standards of the global Hare Krishna movement.
s: Chennai's newest major temple, opened in 2012.
_facts: Also known as Sri Sri Radha Krishna Mandir
Gaudiya Vaishnavism temple dedicated to Krishna and Radha
formally inaugurated 26 April 2012
